what: What predicts the Tier 3 fine-tune's gain: it is binary, not graded
law: A clip either LOCKS ON to its reference or it does not. If the fine-tune reduces the mean input error by >= 40%, it captures 98-117% of the headroom available to it. If the reduction is between 0 and 40%, it captures essentially nothing. If the input error grows, the clip gets worse. There is no middle band in 13 clips.
why_it_is_useful: Lock-on is measured from the input alone, so it needs no truth and can be read on Tier 2 and Tier 3 where truth-based selection is not permitted. Headroom says how much a clip has to give and needs truth, so it may choose which clips to RUN; lock-on says whether the clip collected it and is legal to read when choosing which rollout to SHIP. Together they predict a clip's contribution before it is scored against truth.

is_lock_on_predictable_in_advance.answer: No. Nothing available before the run predicts it.
is_lock_on_predictable_in_advance.hands: two-handed 5 of 9 locked on, one-handed 1 of 4 -- far too small to separate
is_lock_on_predictable_in_advance.counterexamples_that_kill_the_obvious_gu: A low reconstruction floor does not imply lock-on: e18 (3.88 cm), e08 (4.63) and e24 (8.94) all have excellent references and all went backwards. A high floor does not forbid it: e06 locked on at 26.21 cm. A large initial input error does not imply it either: e21 locked on from 116 cm while e17 did not from 99 cm.
is_lock_on_predictable_in_advance.planning_consequence: The arm is a lottery with measured odds and a measured payoff: lock-on happens about 54% of the time (7 of 13) and, when it does, collects ~100% of that clip's headroom. So the expected value of running one clip is about 0.54 x its headroom, and the ONLY lever is to pick the clips with the most headroom -- which is how e03, e25, e01, e29 and e16 were chosen. No cleverer pre-selection is available, and about $0.40 per clip is the price of finding out.
